newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: FOCUS-SLOVAK C.BANK SIGNALS SUPPORT FOR CROWN.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-SLOVAK C.BANK SIGNALS SUPPORT FOR CROWN.

text.p: The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) sent a strong signal on Thursday that it would support the Slovak crown to prevent turmoil on the Czech market from pulling the Slovak currency down.
NBS Treasury Director Frantisek Szulenyi told Reuters the Slovak crown was under control at the moment, but added the bank was ready to "react quickly and support the currency if neccessary".

The Slovak currency was hit by what dealers said were massive sales of Slovak crowns resulting from the fall of the Czech crown earlier in the day. The Slovak crown lost some 45 basis points as about $100 million left the country.
"This (statement) really showed a new direction and helped to calm down the market," said Dusan Svitek, an FX trader at the largest Slovak market player, Slovenska Sporitelna.
Svitek said the crown strengthened by around 25 basis points after the central bank comment and moved to around -0.50 percent versus its mark/dollar basket parity.

"Though further development will still much depend on the Czech crown moves, I see the Slovak crown ranging between parity and one percent in the depreciation sphere, a point at which the central bank could intervene," he said.
The Slovak crown is closely related to the Czech crown since foreign banks often play the two currencies together so the currencies usually move in tandem.
The Czech and Slovak republics used to be united in the Czechoslovak federation which split peacefully in 1993 and the two economies are still very closely linked.
Svitek noted that the NBS sent also a second, indirect, signal to the market through its fixing on Thursday, indicating it would not let the Slovak crown fall too far.
The NBS on Thursday fixed the crown at 32.990 to the dollar and at 19.542 to the mark, implying a deviation of -0.25 percent versus the basket midpoint.
The crown was trading at -0.61 percent at the time of the fixing calculation.
Tibor Fratrik, a dealer at ING Bank, said he saw the run on the Slovak crown earlier on Thursday as pure speculation and not based on fundamentals.

"I would say it was just bargain hunting, in which also some domestic banks were involved," he said. "This decline (of the Slovak crown) seems to me a short-term phenomena which will not set a longer-term trend."
Fratrik said he expected the crown to move between parity and -0.1 percent versus the midpoint and that the central bank appeared content for it to stay within this range.
